(CNN) -- Human rights groups in Bangladesh and abroad are calling for an investigation after 16 borders guards accused of participating in a bloody revolt in February died in custody in recent days. A Bangladesh Rifles soldier is shown wearing a white cloth signifying surrender in late February. The Bangladesh military acknowledged the deaths of the Bangladesh Rifles paramilitary troops, or jawans -- but insisted they were the result of illness and suicide. "Given the history of abuses by security forces in Bangladesh, there is no reason to take at face value the claim that these detainees have committed suicide," said Brad Adams, Asia director or the New York-based Human Rights Watch, in a statement. The 16 were among 1,100 jawans rounded up after a 35-hour mutiny that began on February 25 in the Rifles headquarters in the capital city, Dhaka. The jawans rebelled against their commanding officers, taking dozens of them hostage. When the standoff ended, more than 70 people were found dead -- the majority of them army officers. Initially, Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina promised the jawans amnesty if they laid down their arms. But once the scope of the massacre came to light, Hasina withdrew her offer -- saying the government will not show mercy to those who killed, looted or committed arson. The jawans were issued an ultimatum to turn themselves in, while the government created a committee to probe into the mutiny. The result of the government inquiry is yet to be made public, after several delays. On Thursday, the Rifles leadership issued a statement that said 16 detainees have died in custody since March 9: four from suicide, six from heart attacks and six from other diseases. "We believe that perhaps they have failed to cope with the mental pressure associated with the guilt of committing the brutal attacks,"the statement said. It then added: "Suicide is seen as a sin in religious terms and is also socially undesirable." In response, the legal aid group, Ain o Salish Kendro (Law and Adjudication Center), and the Bangladesh National Women Lawyers' Association were among several organizations calling for an investigation. During a hearing Wednesday, one of the suspects told a Dhaka court he had been administered electric shocks during a seven-day detention. Family members of other detainees have made similar allegations. Some of the suspects who died in custody had wounds on their bodies consisted with torture, Human Rights Watch said. Bangladeshi authorities have said the wounds may have been inflicted when the suspects tried to escape from the Rifles headquarters after the rebellion. "The explanations given by representatives of the security forces are simply not credible," Adams said. "Torture is a regular 'investigative technique' in Bangladesh and killing of detains in government custody is an endemic problem." The country's elite anti-crime unit, Rapid Action Battalion (RAB), have often been accused of 'extra-judicial' killings. The battalion is involved in the interrogation of many of the Rifles suspects. Since its inception in 2004, more than 550 alleged criminals died soon after they were captured by RAB forces. In each case, the battalion claimed the arrested men died from stray bullets as their units were engaged in gun battles with the suspects' comrades. The 65,000-strong Bangladesh Rifles is responsible primarily for guarding the country's borders, but it also takes part in operations such as monitoring polls. It is distinct from the army, but their commanders are career army officers. The troops staged their rebellion on the second day of BDR Week, when officers and troops from various BDR outposts along the border were in the capital for celebrations. Discontent had been bubbling for years in the ranks of the BDR, who complained their army superiors dismissed their appeals for more pay, subsidized food and their requests to participate in United Nations peacekeeping operations -- which pay far more than what they make at home. Bangladesh and its South Asian neighbors are the largest troop contributors to U.N. peacekeeping operations. During the stand-off, dozens of officers were killed. Some bodies were dumped in mass graves. Others were tossed in sewers that emptied into a river, where they floated for miles before being retrieved.

These men had been accused of taking part in a violent uprising back in February. One image from late February depicts a Bangladesh Rifles soldier holding up a white cloth as a sign of his surrender.

Military officials in Bangladesh confirmed that these paramilitary members of the Bangladesh Rifles, known as jawans, had died. However, they maintained that the deaths stemmed from either sickness or suicide.

Brad Adams, who directs Asia operations for the New York-based Human Rights Watch, expressed skepticism in a public statement: "Given the history of abuses by security forces in Bangladesh, there is no reason to take at face value the claim that these detainees have committed suicide."

These 16 individuals were part of a larger group of 1,100 jawans detained following a mutiny that lasted 35 hours and started on February 25 at the Rifles' headquarters located in Dhaka, the nation's capital. The soldiers turned against the officers in charge of them and seized several dozen as captives. By the time the confrontation concluded, over 70 individuals had lost their lives, most of whom were officers in the army.

At first, Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina offered the jawans a pardon on the condition that they surrender their weapons. However, after the full extent of the killings became apparent, she rescinded this offer, declaring that the government would not extend leniency to anyone responsible for murder, theft, or arson. The soldiers were given a deadline to surrender, and a special committee was formed by the government to investigate the uprising. Despite multiple postponements, the findings of this official investigation have still not been released to the public.

The Rifles' leadership released a statement on Thursday indicating that since March 9, a total of 16 people held in custody had died: four by suicide, six from heart attacks, and six from various illnesses. According to the statement, "We believe that perhaps they have failed to cope with the mental pressure associated with the guilt of committing the brutal attacks." It went on to note that "Suicide is seen as a sin in religious terms and is also socially undesirable."

Several organizations responded by demanding an inquiry, among them the legal assistance group Ain o Salish Kendro (Law and Adjudication Center) and the Bangladesh National Women Lawyers' Association.

At a court proceeding on Wednesday, one of the accused informed a Dhaka court that he had endured electric shocks throughout a seven-day period of detention. Relatives of other detained individuals have voiced comparable accusations. According to Human Rights Watch, several of the suspects who perished in custody bore injuries on their bodies that matched signs of torture. Officials in Bangladesh have suggested that these injuries might have occurred when the suspects attempted to flee the Rifles' headquarters in the aftermath of the revolt.

"The explanations given by representatives of the security forces are simply not credible," Adams remarked. "Torture is a regular 'investigative technique' in Bangladesh and killing of detains in government custody is an endemic problem."

Bangladesh's premier anti-crime force, the Rapid Action Battalion (RAB), has frequently faced accusations of carrying out killings outside the legal system. This same unit has been participating in questioning many of the Rifles suspects. Since it was established in 2004, more than 550 people suspected of crimes have died shortly after being taken into RAB custody. In every instance, the battalion asserted that those detained were struck by stray bullets while its units exchanged gunfire with the suspects' associates.

Numbering roughly 65,000 members, the Bangladesh Rifles primarily handles the protection of the country's borders, though it also participates in various duties such as overseeing elections. Although separate from the army, its commanders come from the ranks of professional army officers.

The soldiers launched their rebellion on the second day of BDR Week, a time when officers and personnel from numerous BDR posts positioned along the border had gathered in the capital to take part in festivities. Frustration had been simmering within the BDR for many years. The troops grievance was that their superiors in the army had repeatedly ignored their requests for higher wages, discounted food, and opportunities to join United Nations peacekeeping missions, which offer significantly better compensation than they receive within Bangladesh. Throughout the confrontation, numerous officers were slain. The bodies of some were buried together in mass graves, while others were thrown into sewer systems that drained into a river, where they drifted for considerable distances before being recovered.

# 16 Bangladesh Border Guards Die in Custody Following Deadly Mutiny

**Dhaka, Bangladesh** — Human rights organizations are demanding an independent investigation after 16 members of the Bangladesh Rifles (BDR) died in custody in the months following the February 2009 mutiny that left dozens of army officers dead, raising alarm over the treatment of detained personnel.

The border guards died while being held in connection with the two-day uprising at the BDR headquarters in Dhaka's Pilkhana district, which began on February 25, 2009. The revolt, one of the bloodiest internal security crises in Bangladesh's history, claimed the lives of at least 74 people, including 57 army officers.

## Questions Over Custodial Deaths

Authorities have attributed the deaths to a range of causes, including illness, heart attacks, and in some cases suicide. However, these explanations have been met with skepticism from families of the deceased and international human rights advocates, who point to signs of physical trauma on some bodies.

Rights groups say the pattern of deaths among detainees demands scrutiny, particularly given the large-scale detentions that followed the mutiny. Thousands of BDR soldiers were rounded up in the aftermath as investigators sought to identify those responsible for the killings.

## Human Rights Groups Respond

Human Rights Watch and local organizations have called on the Bangladeshi government to conduct transparent inquiries into each death.

"The deaths of these men in custody raise serious concerns about torture and mistreatment," a Human Rights Watch representative said, urging authorities to ensure that all detainees are treated in accordance with international law and that any allegations of abuse are thoroughly investigated.

Local rights group Odhikar documented multiple cases in which family members reported seeing injuries inconsistent with the official causes of death, and called for medical examinations to be conducted by independent professionals.

## Government Position

Government officials have maintained that detainees are being treated humanely and that deaths in custody are being investigated through proper channels. Officials stressed the scale of the challenge in processing thousands of suspects while pursuing justice for the murdered officers.

Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, whose government took office weeks before the mutiny, faced significant pressure to hold those responsible accountable while managing tensions between the military and civilian leadership.

## A Nation Still Reeling

The mutiny sent shockwaves through Bangladesh and strained relations between the army and the government. In the years that followed, mass trials were held for those accused of participating in the revolt, resulting in numerous convictions and death sentences.

The custodial deaths remain a point of contention for rights advocates, who argue that justice for the victims of the mutiny should not come at the expense of due process for the accused.

"Accountability must work both ways," one activist said. "The victims of the Pilkhana massacre deserve justice, but so do those who may have died from abuse while in state custody."

Human rights organizations continue to press for independent oversight and transparency as legal proceedings unfold.

# The BDR Mutiny Aftermath: Deaths, Allegations, and Government Response

## Background

In February 2009, a mutiny erupted at the Bangladesh Rifles (BDR) headquarters in Pilkhana, Dhaka. Over two days (February 25-26), mutinying border guards killed 74 people, including 57 army officers who had been deputed to lead the paramilitary force. The massacre remains one of the darkest episodes in Bangladesh's post-independence history.

## Detainee Deaths in Custody

Following the mutiny's suppression, thousands of BDR personnel were detained for investigation and trial. Human rights organizations documented a troubling pattern of deaths among these detainees:

- **Custodial deaths:** Numerous BDR soldiers reportedly died while in custody during the investigation period. Rights groups and family members alleged these deaths resulted from torture and mistreatment rather than natural causes cited by authorities.
- **Official explanations:** Authorities typically attributed deaths to illness, heart attacks, or suicide, explanations that families and human rights monitors frequently disputed.

## Torture Allegations

Multiple credible human rights organizations raised serious concerns:

- **Human Rights Watch** and local groups like **Odhikar** documented allegations of systematic torture during interrogations.
- Reports described beatings, denial of medical treatment, and coercive interrogation methods.
- Families reported seeing injuries on the bodies of deceased detainees inconsistent with official cause-of-death claims.
- Concerns were raised about the mass detention process and conditions in overcrowded facilities.

## Judicial and Trial Process

The government pursued justice through multiple tracks:

- **Special tribunals** were established to try thousands of BDR personnel for the mutiny itself.
- **Mass trials** resulted in convictions of large numbers of defendants, raising due process concerns from observers about the fairness of proceedings involving so many accused simultaneously.
- A **separate murder trial** addressed the killings, with death sentences and lengthy prison terms handed down to numerous defendants.

## Government Response

The government's actions included:

- **Disbanding and rebranding:** The BDR was reorganized and renamed the **Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB)** in 2010, accompanied by structural reforms.
- **Official investigations:** Government committees investigated the mutiny's causes, examining grievances over pay, corruption allegations, and command relationships.
- **Defense of custody practices:** Authorities generally denied systematic torture, though the volume of custodial deaths drew sustained criticism.

## Criticism and Ongoing Concerns

Human rights advocates raised persistent concerns about:

- The lack of independent, transparent investigations into custodial deaths.
- Due process shortcomings in mass trials.
- Accountability gaps regarding alleged torture.

---

*Note: For the most current developments—including any renewed investigations following political changes in Bangladesh in 2024—I'd recommend consulting recent reporting from news outlets and human rights organizations, as this remains a subject of ongoing legal and political attention.*

# The 2009 BDR Mutiny: Rebellion, Retribution, and Human Rights Concerns

## Background: A Force Divided

In February 2009, Bangladesh experienced one of the most violent internal security crises in its post-independence history. Over the course of roughly 33 hours beginning on February 25, members of the Bangladesh Rifles (BDR)—the paramilitary border security force—staged a bloody mutiny at their Pilkhana headquarters in Dhaka. By the time it ended, at least 74 people were dead, including 57 army officers who had been seconded to command the force.

## Causes of the Mutiny

The rebellion arose from long-simmering grievances among rank-and-file BDR soldiers, who chafed under a command structure staffed by officers deputed from the regular army. Several factors converged:

- **Pay and conditions:** Ordinary BDR jawans complained of low wages, poor treatment, and inadequate benefits compared to their army counterparts.
- **Perceived corruption:** Resentment centered on allegations that army officers pocketed profits from lucrative operations, including a program known as *Operation Dal-Bhat*, a subsidized food distribution scheme.
- **Career stagnation:** BDR soldiers had limited opportunities for promotion into leadership roles, which were reserved for army officers.

These tensions erupted during the force's annual gathering, known as BDR Week, when the presence of senior officers presented an opportunity for confrontation that quickly spiraled into deadly violence.

## Consequences: A National Crisis

The mutiny presented an early test for the newly installed government of Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, who had taken office weeks earlier. Facing pressure to avoid a full-scale military assault that could have escalated casualties, the government pursued negotiations and offered a conditional amnesty—a decision later criticized when the scale of the killings became apparent.

The aftermath brought sweeping consequences:

- The BDR was disbanded and reconstituted as the **Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB)**.
- Thousands of personnel were arrested and subjected to mass trials.
- The killings deprived the army of a significant portion of its officer corps, straining civil-military relations.

## Custodial Deaths and Legal Proceedings

The government pursued justice through parallel tracks: criminal trials for the murders and separate military-style tribunals for mutiny-related offenses. Tens of thousands of suspects were processed, with special courts handling cases involving large numbers of defendants simultaneously.

It was during the investigative and detention phase that serious allegations emerged. Human rights organizations reported that dozens of detained BDR soldiers died in custody. Rights groups documented that a significant number of these deaths occurred while suspects were being held for interrogation, raising alarms about the conditions and methods used to extract confessions and information.

## Criticism from Human Rights Watch and Legal Aid Groups

**Human Rights Watch (HRW)** became one of the most prominent international critics of the government's handling of the aftermath. In reports and statements, the organization raised concerns including:

- **Deaths in custody:** HRW documented that numerous suspects died while detained, and called for independent investigations into whether torture contributed to these deaths.
- **Allegations of torture:** The group cited accounts suggesting that detainees were mistreated during interrogation.
- **Fair trial concerns:** HRW questioned whether mass trials—processing hundreds or thousands of defendants together—could adequately protect due process rights, including access to legal counsel and the ability to mount an individual defense.

**Domestic legal aid organizations**, including groups such as Ain o Salish Kendra (ASK) and others in Bangladesh's civil society, echoed many of these concerns. They emphasized:

- The difficulty defendants faced in securing adequate legal representation given the enormous scale of the proceedings.
- The reliability of confessions potentially obtained under duress.
- The need for transparent, independent inquiries into custodial deaths.

## The Government's Position

Authorities defended their handling of the crisis, arguing that the gravity of the crimes—the systematic murder of dozens of officers—demanded a firm response. Officials maintained that legal procedures were followed and that the scale of the trials reflected the scale of the rebellion rather than any intent to deny justice. The government also pointed to convictions and death sentences as evidence of accountability for the perpetrators of the killings.

## A Contested Legacy

More than a decade later, the 2009 mutiny remains a deeply contested episode in Bangladesh's history. For the families of the murdered officers, the killings represent an atrocity demanding full accountability. For rights advocates and the families of BDR soldiers who died in custody, the state's response raised troubling questions about torture, due process, and the balance between security imperatives and human rights.

The tension embodied in this case—between the pursuit of justice for a grave crime and the obligation to conduct that pursuit lawfully—continues to define debates over the rule of law in Bangladesh. It stands as a reminder that how a state responds to internal violence can be nearly as consequential as the violence itself.

---

*This piece provides an overview based on widely reported accounts of the 2009 events. Readers seeking detailed information should consult primary sources, including reports from Human Rights Watch, statements from Bangladeshi legal aid organizations, and official government records.*

# Bangladesh Rifles Rebellion: Officers Slain, Jawans Rounded Up, and Questions Over Custodial Deaths

## Background to the Mutiny

The Bangladesh Rifles (BDR) rebellion erupted on February 25, 2009, at the paramilitary force's headquarters at Pilkhana in Dhaka, marking one of the bloodiest internal security crises in the nation's post-independence history. The two-day mutiny left dozens dead, shocked a nation still adjusting to a newly elected democratic government, and set in motion a legal and human rights controversy that would persist for years.

The BDR, a border security force numbering around 67,000 personnel, had long been commanded by officers seconded from the Bangladesh Army. Grievances among the rank-and-file jawans reportedly centered on pay disparities, poor working conditions, allegations of corruption in a subsidized food scheme known as "Operation Dal-Bhat," and resentment toward army officers who commanded the force but did not share its lower ranks' hardships.

## The Rebellion Unfolds

The violence broke out during the annual BDR Week, when senior officers had gathered at the Pilkhana compound. Armed mutineers seized the headquarters, taking officers and their family members hostage. Over the course of roughly 33 hours, the rebellion spread to BDR outposts in other parts of the country.

By the time order was restored, at least 74 people had been killed, including 57 army officers—among them the BDR's Director General, Major General Shakil Ahmed. Many of the officers were shot, and their bodies were later discovered in mass graves within the compound, dumped in sewers, or buried hastily. The brutality of the killings, which included the murder of officers' family members, sent waves of grief and anger through the armed forces and the wider public.

Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, whose Awami League government had taken office only weeks earlier, faced an immediate and delicate crisis. She opted for negotiations, offering an amnesty to the mutineers in an effort to end the standoff without triggering a broader military confrontation. Critics later argued that the delay in deploying the army allowed some perpetrators to escape and destroy evidence, while the government defended the approach as necessary to prevent even greater bloodshed.

## The Roundup of Jawans

In the aftermath, security forces launched a sweeping operation to detain BDR personnel suspected of involvement in the mutiny. Thousands of jawans were rounded up across the country and held in custody as investigators worked to identify those responsible for the killings and the broader rebellion.

The scale of the detentions was enormous. The paramilitary force was subsequently disbanded in its existing form and reconstituted as the Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB), with new leadership, a new flag, and reformed structures intended to address the grievances that had fueled the revolt.

Legal proceedings were pursued on two tracks: special courts martial handled charges of mutiny under military law, while civilian courts prosecuted cases of murder, arson, looting, and related crimes. Thousands of personnel were tried in these proceedings, making them among the largest mass trials in the country's history.

## Controversy Over Deaths in Custody

The most persistent controversy to emerge from the crackdown concerned the deaths of detained jawans while in custody. Human rights organizations, including Bangladeshi group Odhikar and international bodies, raised alarm over reports that dozens of suspects had died during interrogation and detention.

Rights advocates alleged that many of these custodial deaths bore signs of torture, and they questioned the official explanations, which often attributed the deaths to illness, heart attacks, or other natural causes. Families of the deceased in some cases disputed the accounts provided by authorities, pointing to injuries on the bodies and demanding independent investigations.

The controversy placed the government in a difficult position. On one hand, there was intense public and institutional pressure—particularly from the army—to hold the perpetrators of the officers' massacre accountable. On the other, allegations of extrajudicial abuse and custodial deaths threatened to undermine the legitimacy of the entire process and drew condemnation from human rights monitors who insisted that even those accused of grave crimes were entitled to due process and humane treatment.

Human rights groups called for transparent, impartial inquiries into each custodial death, arguing that failure to investigate would signal impunity for abuses by security forces. Authorities generally maintained that deaths in custody were investigated and that many resulted from causes unrelated to mistreatment, though critics remained unconvinced by the official findings.

## Trials and Verdicts

The judicial reckoning stretched over several years. In the mass mutiny trials conducted by special courts, thousands of BDR personnel were convicted and given prison sentences of varying lengths.

The main murder case, concerning the killing of the army officers, culminated in a landmark verdict delivered by a Dhaka court in November 2013. Scores of defendants were sentenced to death, and many others received life imprisonment or lesser terms, while some were acquitted. The verdict was one of the largest of its kind, reflecting both the enormity of the crime and the scale of the prosecution. Appeals and further legal proceedings continued in higher courts in subsequent years, prolonging the legal aftermath of the events at Pilkhana.

## Lasting Impact

The BDR rebellion left deep scars on Bangladesh's institutions and national psyche. The loss of dozens of experienced army officers was a severe blow to the military, and the episode strained relations between the civilian government and the armed forces during a politically sensitive period.

The reconstitution of the border force as the Border Guard Bangladesh represented an attempt to move beyond the crisis and address the underlying grievances, but the questions surrounding custodial deaths, the fairness of the mass trials, and the handling of the initial standoff continued to be debated by human rights advocates, political figures, and the families affected by the tragedy.

More than a decade later, the events of February 2009 remain a defining and contested chapter in Bangladesh's history—remembered both for the horror of the officers' massacre and for the unresolved human rights questions raised by the state's response.
